beats.text: Hi! Meet Q-B and Q-bo, my two cats. They look so alike that my camera can't tell them apart.
I'm at work all day. I just want to know: did they eat, sleep, play? Cats hide illness, so small changes matter.
But here's the catch: last week, my camera decided this exercise ball was Q-bo. For twenty-six minutes!
Why not send every frame to a big AI? We tried: eight minutes of video took an hour and twenty-five dollars, and still missed a cat.
A bigger model on the Pi? It only runs YOLO nano, at three frames a second: almost free, but it makes mistakes.
A bigger detector is out of scope. We keep the small model, and make it smarter with AI. So, we built both.
This is Agentic Realtime Computer Vision: the AI gives the camera a brain, and the camera gives the AI eyes.
Here's how it works. The Pi watches every frame. When it's unsure, our bridge asks Meta's Muse Spark, and remembers what's normal.
And doubts are rare: twelve in eight minutes.
Each doubt has a name. There are fifteen kinds, like: I relabeled this cat by distance alone.
It becomes a plain-English question, with evidence and a strict answer format.
Then the agent pulls the frames it needs, zooms into each cat, and answers with a reason.
Related doubts share a call: twelve questions, just five calls.
Every verdict rewrites the record, and every change is traceable.
Then there's memory. Not boxes and timestamps, but a diary: Q-B slept in the green bed, from four thirty-four to four forty.
Over weeks, it learns what normal looks like, for each cat, in each spot.
So, does it work? The tracker called the sleeping cat Q-bo. The agent saw cool white fur and white paws: that's Q-B. Overturned!
Here, the tracker swapped two cats walking close together. The agent checked both, and swapped them right back.
When the detector itself is wrong, the cat gets relabeled, and that ball becomes a known decoy.
Put together, the same eight minutes tell the true story: Q-B slept the whole time, and Q-bo walked in and out.
The numbers? One percent of frames call the AI, false alarms drop ninety-three percent, and ninety-nine percent of what the camera saw gets the right cat. All for thirty-nine cents!
And cats are just the start: lab mice, tiny drones, cars in fog, production lines. Any small model watching for rare moments has this gap.
Next: run Muse Glimmer locally, give your own agent these eyes, and let its verdicts teach the Pi.
Agentic Realtime Computer Vision. Built this week, on Meta's Muse Spark. Thanks for watching!
